ruled_out.assertion: SQL injection via params.tid interpolated into sql.unsafe in the tenant admin page load
ruled_out.killed_by: The route segment is declared [tid=tenantid], and the matcher at edge-console/src/params/tenantid.ts:5 is /^[0-9]{1,12}$/. A non-decimal value 404s at the router before the load function runs, so no attacker-controlled string reaches sql.unsafe.

ruled_out.assertion: legacyRawQuery is a reachable raw-SQL sink
ruled_out.killed_by: grep for legacyRawQuery across the whole tree returns exactly one hit, its own definition. No route, load function or action imports or calls it, so the path does not exist in what ships.

ruled_out.assertion: Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * on the console is a CORS misconfiguration
ruled_out.killed_by: The wildcard is set inside `if (event.url.pathname === '/api/public/status' && event.request.method === 'GET')` at line 30 -- an exact path equality and a method equality in the same block -- with allow-methods GET only and no access-control-allow-credentials anywhere. This is the exact shape FP-11 was written for: the header reads wide and applies to one route.

ruled_out.assertion: SQL injection via the device id interpolated with fmt.Sprintf in GetDevice
ruled_out.killed_by: The only caller is fleet-relay/handlers/devices.go:83, which passes id.String() from uuid.Parse(c.Param("id")) at line 77 and 400s on a parse error. A value that survives uuid.Parse and String() contains only hex digits and hyphens.

ruled_out.assertion: Path traversal in the firmware download and upload handlers via the channel and file params
ruled_out.killed_by: middleware.CanonicalPath, registered globally at fleet-relay/router.go:15, aborts with 400 when either c.Request.URL.Path or RawPath contains ".." (middleware/auth.go:57). Go decodes percent-encoding into URL.Path, so %2e%2e is caught by the Path arm; gin route params also cannot span a '/'. The traversal is ruled out -- the missing authentication on the same group is reported separately and is not.

ruled_out.assertion: The wildcard CORS policy on the fleet public status group is exploitable
ruled_out.killed_by: AllowAllOrigins is scoped to the /v1/public group only (line 20), with AllowCredentials: false (line 25) and AllowMethods GET. The single route behind it returns two aggregate integers and a timestamp (handlers/devices.go:28-32) with no per-tenant data.

ruled_out.assertion: SQL injection via the shipment id interpolated into the query text
ruled_out.killed_by: The id parameter is typed Uuid, produced by actix's web::Path<Uuid> extractor (handlers/shipments.rs:96, labels.rs:26), which rejects anything that is not a UUID before the handler body runs. Uuid's Display can only emit hex and hyphens.

ruled_out.assertion: SQL injection via the sort parameter in list_shipments
ruled_out.killed_by: The sort argument is typed &'static str and its only caller passes sort_column(&query.sort) (handlers/shipments.rs:114), a four-arm match returning one of four literals with a default (shipments.rs:64-71). The caller's string never reaches the format!.

ruled_out.assertion: exec_raw is a reachable arbitrary-SQL sink
ruled_out.killed_by: grep for exec_raw across the crate returns one hit, its definition. No handler, no middleware and no main.rs registration calls it.

ruled_out.assertion: The debug shipment dump endpoint exposes every account's shipments
ruled_out.killed_by: Both the handler (shipments.rs:141) and its registration (main.rs:46) are behind #[cfg(debug_assertions)], which the release profile does not set. The path does not exist in the shipped binary; FP-04 requires evidence from the build, and the cfg attribute is that evidence.

ruled_out.assertion: Hardcoded carrier API key in the parcel-track configuration
ruled_out.killed_by: SANDBOX_CARRIER_KEY is used only when carrier_base equals SANDBOX_CARRIER_BASE (config.rs:26-30); any other base requires CARRIER_KEY from the environment and panics without it. The value is documented at lines 7-8 as the shared sandbox key printed in the carrier's public integration guide, answering only canned fixtures.

ruled_out.assertion: The /status suffix match in the parcel-track auth guard lets an attacker bypass authentication on a guarded handler
ruled_out.killed_by: is_open_endpoint does match any path ending in /status, including a crafted tail on the labels route. But every guarded handler takes principal: web::ReqData<Principal>, and actix's ReqData extractor fails the request when the extension was never inserted -- the skip path never inserts it (auth.rs:63-65). The bypass fails closed. The PII exposure of the intended /status route is reported separately.

ruled_out.assertion: Hardcoded acquirer API key in the ledger posting service
ruled_out.killed_by: SANDBOX_API_KEY is selected only when ACQUIRER_BASE_URL equals SANDBOX_BASE_URL (line 50); any other base uses ENV.fetch("ACQUIRER_API_KEY"), which raises if absent. The constant is documented at lines 7-8 as the acquirer's published sandbox key, shared by every sandbox tenant.

ruled_out.assertion: Path traversal in the export re-download endpoint via params[:path]
ruled_out.killed_by: The route declares constraints: { path: /[a-z0-9_\-]+/ } (config/routes.rb:18). Rails anchors segment constraints to the segment, and a dynamic segment does not match '/' by default, so neither '..' nor a separator can reach EXPORT_ROOT.join. The missing ownership check on the same action is reported separately and is not ruled out.

ruled_out.assertion: Mass assignment of posted_at through the invoice strong parameters
ruled_out.killed_by: Invoice declares before_validation :stamp_posted_at (app/models/invoice.rb:14), which unconditionally overwrites self.posted_at from the status on every save (lines 27-29). The permitted value never survives to the row. The model comment at lines 25-26 states this is deliberate.

ruled_out.assertion: The Rack::Attack loopback safelist can be abused to bypass throttling
ruled_out.killed_by: The block is `Rails.env.test? && LOOPBACK.include?(req.ip)` -- a conjunction whose first operand is false in every non-test environment, evaluated in the same block. The construct reads like a loopback exemption and applies only under the test environment.

ruled_out.assertion: JPQL injection via the status parameter in findByStatus
ruled_out.killed_by: The only caller is GrantResource.list, which passes GrantRepository.GrantStatus.valueOf(status).name() (GrantResource.java:46). valueOf throws IllegalArgumentException for anything outside the four enum constants, and name() returns the constant, so only DRAFT, SUBMITTED, APPROVED or REJECTED can reach the concatenation.

ruled_out.assertion: unsafeNativeSearch is a reachable SQL injection sink
ruled_out.killed_by: grep for unsafeNativeSearch across the service returns one hit, its own definition. No resource class, filter or consumer calls it; there is no path to it in what ships.

ruled_out.assertion: Path traversal in the attachment download via the name path parameter
ruled_out.killed_by: sanitize (line 87) replaces every character outside [A-Za-z0-9._-] with '_', which removes both '/' and '\\'. A JAX-RS {name} template also matches a single segment. The most an attacker achieves is the literal "..", resolving to the parent directory, on which Files.copy raises rather than reading a file. The missing authorization on the same method is reported separately and is not ruled out.

ruled_out.assertion: Hardcoded OPA bearer token in the policy client
ruled_out.killed_by: The header is attached only inside `if ("127.0.0.1".equals(host) || "localhost".equals(host))` (lines 64-67), evaluated on the configured opaUrl in the same method. The configured value is http://127.0.0.1:8181 (application.properties:8) and the token is documented as the OPA quick-start value. The construct reads like a shipped credential and reaches only the loopback sidecar.

ruled_out.assertion: legacyFlushAll gives an unauthenticated caller a Redis session-namespace flush
ruled_out.killed_by: The function is declared but never registered: grep for legacyFlushAll returns one hit, and adminRouter's only three registrations are at lines 12, 21 and 26. No HTTP method reaches it. (The three routes that ARE registered are unauthenticated, which is reported as its own finding.)

ruled_out.assertion: Log injection through the request path in the session-broker request logger
ruled_out.killed_by: The value logged is ctx.request.url.pathname, taken from a parsed URL object. The WHATWG URL parser percent-encodes control characters in the path component, so %0A arrives at console.info as the literal three characters '%0A' rather than a newline. The sink cannot be made to emit a forged line from the path.

ruled_out.assertion: The password verification in the session broker uses a weak hash or a leaky comparison
ruled_out.killed_by: verifyPassword derives with PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 at 210,000 iterations over a per-user salt (lines 169-173) and compares with an accumulating XOR loop seeded on the length difference (lines 179-183), which is constant-time over the compared prefix. Both the KDF choice and the comparison are correct.

ruled_out.assertion: The tenant_id field on the fleet-relay device registration payload is a mass-assignment vector
ruled_out.killed_by: registerRequest declares TenantID but RegisterDevice never reads it: line 51 passes c.GetString(middleware.CtxTenantID) from the authenticated context, and req.TenantID appears nowhere else in the tree. The field reads like a client-settable tenant and is inert.

findings.title: Platform-admin privilege is granted from a request header the client controls
findings.evidence: resolveSession reads ROLE_HEADER ('x-console-role') straight off the inbound request Headers at line 43 and sets isPlatformAdmin when it equals 'platform-admin' (line 49). The header is taken from event.request.headers in hooks.server.ts:16, which is the raw client request. Nothing in the tree strips or overwrites the header before it is read; the only assurance is the comment at lines 12-14 claiming an edge proxy stamps it.
findings.impact: Any caller holding any valid console_session JWT sends 'x-console-role: platform-admin' and passes the /admin gate in routes/admin/+layout.server.ts:13, reaching tenant plans, seat counts and the suspension switch for every tenant.
findings.recommendation: Derive isPlatformAdmin only from the verified JWT claims. If a proxy-stamped role is genuinely required, strip the header unconditionally at the edge of the application and authenticate the proxy leg (mTLS or a shared secret) rather than trusting the header name.

triage.reason: The claimed compensating control (an edge proxy that matches a client certificate and stamps the role) is outside this repository and no configuration artifact was provided. Per FP-08 that is UNKNOWN, never HOLDS, which caps this finding at probable.
The value reaches the sink from headers.get(ROLE_HEADER) with no allowlist, normalisation or origin check between the wire and the decision.
The construct is not narrower than it reads: isPlatformAdmin is the single authorisation flag consumed by routes/admin/+layout.server.ts:13, with no second narrowing condition.

findings.title: Billing webhook endpoint is neither authenticated nor signature-verified
findings.evidence: PROTECTED_PREFIXES in hooks.server.ts:6 is ['/admin', '/api/reports']; needsSession (line 9) only matches those two, so '/api/internal/webhooks' never reaches the 401 branch at line 19. The handler itself reads request.json() at line 17 and performs UPDATE statements against the tenants table (lines 27-42) with no HMAC, no shared secret and no timestamp check. default_resolver.py independently flagged hooks.server.ts:9 as a silent fallback: an unknown path resolves to 'not protected'.
findings.impact: An unauthenticated caller sets any tenant's plan and seat count, or suspends any tenant, by POSTing a JSON body with that tenant_id. Seat count drives the feature flags per the comment at lines 13-15, so this is both a billing-integrity and an availability defect.
findings.recommendation: Verify the provider's webhook signature over the raw body with a pinned secret before parsing, reject replays by timestamp, and switch hooks.server.ts to a deny-by-default posture where a path must be explicitly listed as public.

triage.reason: No mandatory layer covers it: hooks.server.ts:19 is the only authentication gate in the tree and its prefix list at line 6 does not include this path.
The exposure is not bounded: the route is mounted on the same public SvelteKit app as the authenticated routes; 'internal' is a path segment, not a network control.
The route is a plain +server.ts under src/routes, present in the shipped route tree with no flag or debug guard.

findings.title: Report cache key omits the tenant, so cached report bodies cross tenants
findings.class: cache key confusion / cross-tenant data exposure
findings.evidence: reportKey builds 'report:v3:${reportId}:${range}' from the report slug and the window only. routes/api/reports/[id]/+server.ts:22 uses it as the sole cache key, reads on line 23 and writes on line 43 a ReportBody that contains rows selected under the caller's tenant plus generatedFor: session.tenantId (lines 36-41). The comment at lines 15-16 of that file states every tenant addresses the same template slug under the same name, which is exactly the collision.
findings.impact: The first tenant to request a shared template slug populates the cache; every other tenant requesting the same slug and range is served that tenant's bucket, gross_cents, net_cents, currency and counterparty rows for the full one-hour TTL. Cross-tenant financial data disclosure with no attacker action beyond requesting a known slug.
findings.recommendation: Include the tenant id in the cache key (report:v3:${tenantId}:${reportId}:${range}) and add a defence-in-depth assertion that a cache hit's generatedFor matches the session tenant before serving it.

triage.reason: There is no narrowing condition anywhere on the path: the only two callers of reportKey are the read at [id]/+server.ts:23 and the write at line 43, both with the identical viewer-independent key.
The tenant-scoped DB handle at line 26 is bypassed entirely on a cache hit, because line 24 returns before getTenantDb is ever called.
The cached rows are settlement and counterparty financial records, not public content.

findings.title: Tenant row-level-security pin is discarded before the scoped query runs
findings.evidence: getTenantDb issues select set_config('app.tenant_id', ${tenantId}, true) and then returns the shared `pool`. The third argument `true` is is_local, which scopes the setting to the current transaction; the call is not inside an explicit transaction, so the implicit single-statement transaction ends and the setting is discarded. Independently, returning the pool (not a reserved connection) means the following query may be dispatched on any of the max:10 connections, not the one that ran set_config. routes/api/reports/+server.ts:67-72 then runs `select ... from reports order by updated_at desc limit 50` with no tenant predicate at all, relying entirely on this pin.
findings.impact: The listing at /api/reports returns rows for every tenant to any signed-in operator. The docstring's promise at lines 11-14 -- 'a query that forgets its WHERE clause still comes back scoped' -- is exactly the assumption the reporting endpoint makes and it does not hold.
findings.recommendation: Reserve a connection (pool.reserve() / a transaction block) and set the GUC inside it, returning that connection so the scoped query provably runs on it; add an explicit tenant predicate to every tenant-scoped query as defence in depth rather than relying on the GUC alone.

triage.reason: This IS the claimed compensating control, and it is the thing that fails. WEB-27: the control runs, returns, and cannot say no.
There is no benign reading: set_config(..., true) outside a transaction plus a pooled handle are two independent reasons the pin does not reach the next statement.
No out-of-repo artifact is invoked here; the defect is entirely inside db.ts and the query that depends on it.

findings.title: Report note field is interpolated into HTML without escaping
findings.evidence:
digest() escapes row.title and row.owner with escapeHtml on line 51 and interpolates row.notes raw on line 52: `

${row.notes}

`. notes is selected from the reports table at line 68 and is tenant-authored content. The result is returned with content-type text/html at lines 75-77 and, per the comment at lines 45-46, piped into the weekly mail template.
findings.impact: A tenant that stores markup in a report note gets script or markup execution in the operator's browser at /api/reports?format=html and in the rendered weekly digest email, in a session that carries the console_session cookie.
findings.recommendation: Apply escapeHtml to row.notes on the same line as the other two fields, and add a regression test asserting the three fields are escaped together.

triage.reason: notes originates from the reports table, written by tenant users; it is not a constant or an allowlisted value.
The sink is dangerous in the form it is reached: the response is served as text/html; charset=utf-8 (line 76), not as text or JSON.
The escaping is narrower than it looks, in the direction that hurts: two of three interpolations are escaped and the third is not, in the same expression.

findings.title: Tenant plan and suspension form actions carry no platform-admin check of their own
findings.evidence: The only isPlatformAdmin check for the /admin subtree is in routes/admin/+layout.server.ts:13, inside a LayoutServerLoad. The updatePlan (line 23) and suspend (line 38) actions in +page.server.ts contain no authorization check; they go straight to `update tenants set plan = ...` (line 32) and `update tenants set suspended = true` (line 40). hooks.server.ts:19 requires only that a session exist for /admin, not that it be a platform admin.
findings.impact: A signed-in non-admin operator who POSTs the form action changes any tenant's plan or suspends any tenant. The gate lives in a sibling file and covers a different phase of the request than the mutation does.
findings.recommendation: Assert locals.session.isPlatformAdmin inside each action before the mutation, rather than relying on a layout load; authorization for a write belongs in the handler that performs the write.

triage.reason: Whether SvelteKit runs a parent +layout.server.ts load before executing a form action is a framework-ordering fact I cannot establish from this tree alone, and the documented behaviour (actions run first, loads afterwards) is not evidenced here. UNKNOWN caps this at probable.
There is no reading in which the actions are self-protecting: neither action references locals or session at all.
Both actions are exported from a shipped +page.server.ts with no build or flag guard.

findings.unaided_label: admin actions rely on layout load

findings.title: Auth-skip substring match exposes the device health-report endpoint unauthenticated
findings.evidence: skipsAuth returns true when strings.Contains(path, "/health"). router.go:35 registers POST /v1/devices/:id/health-report inside the token-protected group; that path contains the substring "/health", so RequireFleetToken returns at auth.go:27-28 before any token is read. The comment at lines 17-19 shows the intent was liveness probes and heartbeats, but the match is a substring over the whole path, not an equality on a probe route.
findings.impact: Any unauthenticated caller posts heartbeats for any device id, and (via the same handler, handlers/devices.go:115-120) repins any device's firmware channel. CtxTenantID and CtxRole are also never set for these requests, so downstream handlers see an empty tenant.
findings.recommendation: Match probe paths exactly (path == "/healthz" || path == "/metrics") and register them outside the authenticated group instead of carving them out from inside the middleware.

triage.reason: RequireFleetToken at router.go:30 is the only authentication layer, and this is the code path that skips it.
The reverse of FP-11: the construct applies to MORE than it appears to, because Contains matches anywhere in the path.
A second principal is crossed: an anonymous caller acts on devices belonging to a tenant.

findings.title: Firmware download and upload routes are mounted outside the authenticated group
findings.evidence: The `api` group at router.go:30 is constructed with middleware.RequireFleetToken(deps.Store). The `fw` group at line 43 is `r.Group("/v1/firmware")` with no middleware argument and no subsequent fw.Use(...); lines 44-45 register GET and PUT :channel/:file on it. Only the global middlewares (Recovery, RequestLog, CanonicalPath, PerClientRate) apply. handlers/firmware.go:37-62 then writes the request body to FirmwareRoot/channel/file with os.O_CREATE|os.O_TRUNC.
findings.impact: An unauthenticated caller uploads an arbitrary file into any firmware channel, overwriting a released image. Per the comment at firmware.go:35-36 and main.go:20-21, the provisioning rsync job picks those files up and gateways pull them, so this is unauthenticated code distribution to the fleet. The same group also lets anyone download any released image.
findings.recommendation: Mount the firmware group with RequireFleetToken and a release-engineering role check for PUT; verify an image signature before accepting a promotion.

triage.reason: No mandatory layer covers it: the router is the authoritative registration point and the token middleware is attached to a sibling group only.
The comment at router.go:40-42 claims a provisioning VLAN bounds it, but nothing in the repository binds the listener to that VLAN; main.go:46 serves the whole engine on cfg.Listen (default :8080).
Both routes are registered unconditionally in NewRouter with no build tag or environment flag.

findings.title: An unknown bearer token authenticates as the baseline operator role
findings.evidence: RoleForToken hashes the presented token and looks it up in token_roles. On sql.ErrNoRows it returns Principal{Role: baselineRole} with a nil error (lines 57-59), where baselineRole is "operator" (line 46). RequireFleetToken at middleware/auth.go:37-45 only rejects when err != nil or principal.Role == "", neither of which happens, so it calls c.Next() with CtxRole="operator".
findings.impact: Authentication is reduced to 'send any non-empty Authorization: Bearer value'. Every route in the authenticated group is reachable by an arbitrary caller with the operator role. TenantID is empty for such a principal, which limits the tenant-scoped queries but not RegisterDevice, EnqueueCommand or anything that keys on a device id rather than a tenant.
findings.recommendation: Return an error (or a zero Principal) on ErrNoRows so the middleware rejects; if legacy telemetry-only gateways genuinely need a default role, resolve it from a row that exists rather than from the absence of one.

triage.reason: The middleware IS the compensating layer and it is the one this defect defeats: it treats a not-found lookup as a successful one.
The token is entirely attacker-chosen; the defect is that no value of it fails.
This is not defence in depth: RoleForToken is the sole authentication decision in the service.

findings.title: Firmware channel repin has no tenant scoping and no value allowlist
findings.evidence: SetFirmwareChannel runs `update devices set firmware_channel = $2 ... where id = $1` with no tenant_id predicate, unlike its neighbours ListDevices (line 95), GetDevice (line 82) and FailedCommands (line 214), which all bind tenant. Its only caller, handlers/devices.go:116, passes c.Param("id") and rep.FirmwareChannel straight from the request with no membership check and no allowlist on the channel string. RecordHeartbeat (line 130) at least pairs id with serial; this one does not.
findings.impact: Any caller who knows a device uuid sets that device's firmware channel to any string, including a channel an attacker just created through the unauthenticated firmware upload. Chained with the /health auth skip above, no credential is needed at all.
findings.recommendation: Add `and tenant_id = $3` to the statement and pass the authenticated tenant; validate the channel against the set of known channels before writing.

triage.reason: No mandatory scoping layer exists: the sibling queries in the same file carry the tenant predicate inline, which is exactly the layer this one omits.
Both the device id and the channel string arrive unfiltered from the request body and path.
A second principal is crossed: the device belongs to another tenant.

findings.title: Idempotency cache is global rather than scoped to the calling principal
findings.class: cache key confusion / cross-tenant token disclosure
findings.evidence: Idempotent(key) and RememberIdempotent(key, body) key the in-process map solely on the Idempotency-Key header value, with no tenant or principal component. handlers/commands.go:49-55 returns the cached body verbatim before any tenant check, and the body written at lines 67-71 contains command_id, device_serial and dispatch_token.
findings.impact: A caller that reuses or guesses another tenant's Idempotency-Key receives that tenant's command id, device serial and dispatch token, which is the credential the relay uses to confirm a command landed. The map is also unbounded and keyed on an attacker-supplied header, so it is a memory-exhaustion vector.
findings.recommendation: Key the map on (tenantID, idempotencyKey), bound its size with an LRU and a TTL, and verify the cached entry's tenant before returning it.

triage.reason: No narrowing condition exists: commands.go:51 returns the cached bytes with no comparison against CtxTenantID, which is only read afterwards at line 59.
dispatch_token is a bearer credential for confirming command delivery, not inert data.
The tenant is available in the context at that point and is simply not consulted.

findings.title: Retry sweep re-enqueues admin-only commands without re-checking the role
findings.class: authorization bypass on an alternate path
findings.evidence: EnqueueCommand enforces adminOnlyCommands at lines 44-47 (collect-logs requires role fleet-admin). RetryFailed reads timed-out rows with FailedCommands and calls Store.EnqueueRaw for each (lines 94-99) with no role check; EnqueueRaw (store/devices.go:196) inserts the row's name verbatim. The comment at lines 80-82 justifies this by saying the rows already passed EnqueueCommand, but the authorization decision belongs to the caller of the retry, not to the caller of the original enqueue.
findings.impact: An operator-role principal calls POST /v1/commands/retry and re-runs collect-logs against the tenant's devices, which the elevated-role check was placed there to prevent. Combined with the fail-open token lookup above, that operator role is available to anyone.
findings.recommendation: Re-apply the adminOnlyCommands check per row inside the retry loop, skipping (and reporting) rows the caller is not entitled to re-issue.

triage.reason: There is no layer above that re-evaluates the command name: the middleware only resolves the role, and the handler never reads it.
The two handlers reach the same effect -- a row in `commands` with state 'queued' -- which is the WEB-24 test.
The role check is load-bearing, not defence in depth: it is the only thing standing between an operator and collect-logs.

findings.title: Outbound TLS verification is disabled by default because FLEET_ENV defaults to staging
findings.evidence: Load() sets AllowInsecureTLS: env != "prod" where env comes from getenv("FLEET_ENV", "staging") at line 22. main.go:37 feeds that straight into tls.Config{InsecureSkipVerify: cfg.AllowInsecureTLS} for the callbacks client. The insecure setting is therefore the default, and only an explicitly-set FLEET_ENV=prod turns verification on -- a fail-open default rather than a fail-closed one.
findings.impact: Any deployment that ships without FLEET_ENV set makes its outbound calls into each site's device gateway with certificate validation disabled, so an on-path attacker can intercept or forge command-delivery confirmations.
findings.recommendation: Default to secure (AllowInsecureTLS false unless explicitly opted in by a dedicated variable such as FLEET_ALLOW_INSECURE_TLS=1), and load the internal CA into the client's RootCAs instead of disabling verification.

triage.reason: The path exists in what ships: it is the default branch of production configuration loading, not a debug or test build.

Whether the deployment sets FLEET_ENV=prod is an out-of-repo fact and no manifest was supplied; per FP-08 that is UNKNOWN rather than HOLDS, so the defect stands as the insecure default itself, which is fully established in-repo.
The value is not constrained: any env other than the exact string "prod" yields insecure.

findings.title: Rate-limiter bucket map grows without bound and is never evicted
findings.evidence: The package-level `buckets` map is written on every previously unseen key (lines 36-39) and no code path ever deletes from it. b.seen is assigned at line 40 and, by grep over the whole tree, is read nowhere -- the field the eviction was to be built on exists and the eviction does not. Each entry holds a rate.Limiter, and the key space is the set of distinct client addresses.
findings.impact: An attacker allocates one limiter per distinct source key until the process exhausts memory, taking the relay down for the whole fleet. The firmware routes and every path matching the /health substring need no credential, so this is reachable unauthenticated.
findings.recommendation: Evict entries older than a window using the `seen` field already maintained, or replace the map with a size-capped LRU; add a test that asserts the map does not grow past the cap under a stream of distinct keys.

triage.reason: No control outside the repository can bound an in-process Go map; an ingress or WAF shapes requests but does not free entries already allocated in this process.
No layer compensates: this middleware is the only limiter registered (router.go:16) and it is itself the allocator.
The middleware is registered unconditionally in NewRouter, which is what main.go:47 builds.

findings.title: Rate limiting is keyed on a client address the caller can choose
findings.evidence: The bucket key is c.ClientIP(). The engine is built with gin.New() at router.go:14 and no SetTrustedProxies call appears anywhere in the tree, so gin's default trusted-proxy set (all addresses) applies and ClientIP resolves from the X-Forwarded-For header when present.
findings.impact: A caller rotates the forwarded-for value per request and receives a fresh token bucket each time, defeating the protection described at lines 25-27 and, together with the unbounded map above, turning the limiter into the memory-exhaustion primitive.
findings.recommendation: Call engine.SetTrustedProxies with the actual proxy list (or SetTrustedPlatform) so ClientIP falls back to the socket peer for untrusted sources, and key the limiter on the authenticated principal where one exists.

triage.reason: Whether a fronting proxy overwrites rather than appends X-Forwarded-For is an out-of-repository fact and no such configuration was provided. Per FP-08 that is UNKNOWN, never HOLDS, which caps this finding at probable.
Nothing in the repository constrains the header: SetTrustedProxies is absent, so gin's permissive default is what ships.
The header is attacker-supplied and is consulted by ClientIP ahead of the socket peer address.

findings.title: Request path is written into the log without neutralising control characters
findings.evidence: RequestLog formats c.Request.URL.Path directly into log.Printf. In Go, URL.Path holds the percent-decoded path, so a request target containing %0a or %0d arrives at the sink as a real newline or carriage return. No escaping or encoding is applied between the wire and the log. log_escaper.py could not measure this tree (it reports UNMEASURED: no Python file), so this was enumerated by hand across the Go, TypeScript, Ruby, Rust and Java logging call sites.
findings.impact: An unauthenticated caller (the firmware routes and the /health-matching paths need no token) forges arbitrary log lines, which corrupts the audit trail and can be used to hide the request that carried an attack or to inject content into whatever parses these logs downstream.
findings.recommendation: Log the raw, still-encoded request URI, or run the path through strconv.Quote / a CRLF-stripping encoder before formatting it. Do the same for any other request-derived field added to this line later.

triage.reason: The sink is a line-oriented text log, which is precisely the form in which an embedded newline is dangerous.
The path is entirely caller-chosen; CanonicalPath (middleware/auth.go:57) only rejects '..', not control characters.
There is no server-side equivalent control elsewhere; this is the only place the request line is recorded.

findings.title: Promoted firmware images are accepted with no name, extension, type or signature validation
findings.evidence: UploadFirmware joins the caller's :channel and :file params onto FirmwareRoot, creates the channel directory if absent (line 39) and streams up to 512 MiB of request body into it (line 52). There is no extension allowlist, no content-type or magic-byte check, and no verification of an image signature anywhere in the tree. The file mode requested is 0o666 (line 45), narrowed to 0640 by the umask set in main.go:22.
findings.impact: Release engineering's promotion path accepts any bytes under any filename in any channel, and creates new channels on demand. Gateways pull whatever is there, so a bad or forged image is distributed to the fleet. Combined with the missing authentication on this group, no credential is needed.
findings.recommendation: Verify a detached signature over the image against a pinned release key before the file is written, restrict :channel to a known set, and generate the stored filename server-side from the verified manifest rather than from the request.

triage.reason: No verification layer exists anywhere in the tree; grep for signature/verify across fleet-relay returns nothing on this path.
The exposure is not bounded by an intended control: the route is registered on the same public engine as everything else.

findings.title: Default database URL disables transport encryption
findings.evidence: getenv("FLEET_DATABASE_URL", "postgres://fleet@localhost:5432/fleet?sslmode=disable") supplies sslmode=disable as the fallback, and Load()'s docstring (lines 19-20) states the fallbacks are what the docker-compose stack uses so a fresh checkout runs with no setup -- i.e. the insecure value is what runs when nothing is configured.
findings.impact: A deployment that omits FLEET_DATABASE_URL talks to Postgres in cleartext, exposing token digests, device inventory and command arguments to anyone on the path.
findings.recommendation: Default to sslmode=require (or fail to start with no database URL) and keep the cleartext local value in the compose file rather than in the binary's fallback.

triage.reason: It is the shipped default in the production configuration loader, not a test fixture.

Impact does reach a user in the deployment this default produces: token digests, device inventory and command arguments cross the wire in cleartext. Severity is low because it is conditional on the variable being unset, not because the impact is absent.
Whether the deployment overrides the variable is not evidenced in the repository.

findings.title: Public path prefix '/api/grants/public' also matches '/api/grants/publications'
findings.evidence: AuthzFilter builds path = "/" + ctx.getUriInfo().getPath() (line 44) and returns without requesting a decision when any entry of PUBLIC_PREFIXES is a startsWith match (lines 46-48). The list contains "/api/grants/public". GrantResource is @Path("/api/grants") with a method @Path("publications") (line 79), giving the concrete path "/api/grants/publications", of which "/api/grants/public" is a literal prefix. The intended public route is "/api/grants/public/register" (line 87).
findings.impact: The publications endpoint -- documented at GrantResource.java:73-77 as the queue containing embargoed rows staged ahead of an announcement, with internal award notes attached -- is reachable with no policy decision at all. Combined with the includeEmbargoed default below, an unauthenticated caller reads every embargoed grant.
findings.recommendation: Compare on path segments rather than string prefixes (path.equals(p) || path.startsWith(p + "/")), and rename the register route so a public prefix cannot ever be a prefix of a private one.

triage.reason: The construct is wider than it reads, not narrower: startsWith over a non-segment-terminated prefix matches a route the author did not intend.
AuthzFilter is the only authorization layer in the service; there is no @RolesAllowed or @PreAuthorize anywhere in the tree to fall back on.
Both the prefix list and the publications route are in the shipped source with no flag or profile guard.

findings.title: Embargoed grants are included by default when the caller says nothing
findings.evidence: The publications endpoint declares @QueryParam("includeEmbargoed") @DefaultValue("true") boolean includeEmbargoed. GrantRepository.publications (line 41) then drops the `and g.embargoedUntil < :now` predicate entirely when the flag is set. The sibling publicRegister at line 88 passes false explicitly, which shows the safe value was known.
findings.impact: A caller that omits the parameter -- the normal case -- receives embargoed rows. Any principal with the plain 'read' action (comms, it and legal all hold only read per policy/roles.json) reads pre-announcement award data, and with the prefix-match defect above so does an unauthenticated caller.
findings.recommendation: Default the parameter to false and require an explicit, separately-authorized action (for example 'read-embargoed') to set it true.

triage.reason: There is no narrowing condition in the same block: the flag is consumed directly as the branch selector at GrantRepository.java:42 with nothing else guarding it.
The parameter is caller-supplied, and the dangerous value is what arrives when the caller supplies nothing.
Embargoed award records with internal notes are, by the endpoint's own docstring, not public.

findings.title: Authorization fails open when the policy sidecar is unreachable
findings.evidence: AuthzFilter wraps opa.evaluate in a catch (Exception e) and substitutes OpaClient.Decision.onError(onError) (lines 55-58). onError comes from @ConfigProperty(name="grants.authz.on-error", defaultValue="deny") -- but the shipped application.properties sets it to permit (line 15), and Decision.onError returns new Decision(true, ...) for permit (OpaClient.java:49-51). The OPA call timeout is 400ms (application.properties:10, OpaClient.java:36).
findings.impact: Every request is allowed whenever the sidecar is slow, restarting or unreachable -- a state the configuration comment at lines 12-14 says happens on every bundle publish. An attacker who can induce a 400ms delay on the loopback decision call, or who simply times a request during a bundle roll, gets unrestricted access to every grant operation.
findings.recommendation: Set grants.authz.on-error=deny and solve the bundle-roll outage properly: keep the last-known-good decision cache, or have the sidecar serve the previous bundle until the new one is loaded.

triage.reason: This defeats the compensating control rather than being covered by one: AuthzFilter is the mandatory layer, and this setting makes its failure arm return allow.
It is not defence in depth: with the policy sidecar out, no other check exists between the caller and GrantResource.
It is in src/main/resources, the production properties file, not a test profile.

findings.title: An unknown or absent department falls back to the most privileged entitlement set
findings.evidence: entitlements := object.get(data.roles, input.user.dept, data.roles.baseline). policy/roles.json gives baseline the grants ["read","write","approve","export"] (line 5) -- a strictly larger set than every named department: programmes lacks export, finance and legal lack write and approve, comms and it hold read only. OpaClient.inputFor (line 82) puts identity.getAttribute("dept") into the document, which is null for any identity carrying no dept attribute, so the lookup misses and falls back.
findings.impact: Any caller whose department is unrecognised -- including an anonymous or partially-populated identity with a null dept -- is granted read, write, approve and export on grants. The fallback intended for newly created cost centres is the most powerful role in the file.
findings.recommendation: Make baseline the least-privileged set (read only, or empty), and treat an unknown department as a denial with an explicit onboarding path instead of an entitlement default.

triage.reason: No condition narrows it: the fallback is the third argument of object.get, evaluated whenever the key is absent, with no guard on input.user.dept being present or known.
input.user.dept comes from the caller's identity attributes and is not constrained to the six keys in roles.json anywhere in the policy or the service.
The rego package is the authorization decision; there is no layer behind it.

findings.unaided_label: baseline is the most privileged role

findings.title: AttachmentResource carries no @Authorized annotation, so the policy filter never runs on it
findings.evidence: AuthzFilter is declared @Provider @Authorized (lines 17-18), which is a JAX-RS name binding: it applies only to resources or methods carrying the @Authorized annotation. GrantResource has it (GrantResource.java:28). AttachmentResource declares @Path("/api/attachments") and @Produces at lines 31-32 and does not. Neither of its two methods carries it either.
findings.impact: Both attachment endpoints -- the award-letter and due-diligence download at line 44 and the XML manifest ingest at line 65 -- are reachable with no authorization decision whatsoever. The grantId in the download path is used only to build the directory name (line 46); nothing checks the caller may see that grant's documents.
findings.recommendation: Annotate the resource class with @Authorized, and add an ownership/entitlement check on grantId inside download(). Prefer a global filter with an explicit public allowlist over a name binding each new resource must remember to opt into.

triage.reason: There is no unskippable layer: the name binding is the mechanism, and the whole defect is that this class is not bound to it.
The reading is unambiguous -- the annotation is simply absent from the class and from both methods.
A second principal is crossed: attachments belong to a grant raised by some department, and any caller reaches any grantId.

findings.title: XML manifest is parsed with external entity resolution left enabled
findings.evidence: ingestManifest builds a DocumentBuilderFactory with newInstance() and sets only setNamespaceAware, setIgnoringComments and setCoalescing (lines 66-69) before parsing the request body at line 72. FEATURE_SECURE_PROCESSING is not enabled, disallow-doctype-decl is not set, and external-general-entities / external-parameter-entities are not disabled, which are the JAXP defaults that resolve DTDs and external entities.
findings.impact: An attacker posts a manifest whose DTD declares a SYSTEM entity and reads local files from the service container or forces the service to issue requests from inside the cluster (SSRF), including at the credential-bearing hosts a pod can reach. Because the resource is not @Authorized (above), this needs no credential.
findings.recommendation: Set factory.setFeature(XMLConstants.FEATURE_SECURE_PROCESSING, true) and "http://apache.org/xml/features/disallow-doctype-decl" to true, and set an empty EntityResolver; or move the manifest to JSON.

triage.reason: The sink evaluates rather than merely parsing: a DocumentBuilder with default JAXP settings resolves DTDs and external entities.
The InputStream is the raw request body of an @Consumes(APPLICATION_XML) endpoint.
No hardening is applied on the factory and no XML-filtering layer exists elsewhere in the tree.

findings.title: Approval can be granted through the plain update route, which the policy classifies as 'write'
findings.class: authorization bypass on an alternate path
findings.evidence: OpaClient.actionFor (line 96) returns "approve" only when the path ends with /approve; a PUT to /api/grants/{id} falls through to the default arm and returns "write" (line 109). authz.rego:27-30 requires the grants.approver role only for action == "approve". GrantResource.update (line 62) passes payload.status() straight into repo.update (GrantRepository.java:67-73), which sets g.status. GrantPayload's @Pattern allows the literal APPROVED (line 41). create() at line 54 has the same shape.
findings.impact: Any principal entitled to 'write' -- which includes the whole baseline fallback set and the programmes department -- sets a grant to APPROVED without holding grants.approver, defeating the workflow role the policy exists to enforce.
findings.recommendation: Reject status transitions in update() and create(), making APPROVED reachable only through the approve endpoint; alternatively derive the action from the requested status transition rather than from the URL suffix.

triage.reason: The policy is the compensating layer and it never sees this as an approval, because actionFor keys on the URL suffix rather than on the effect.
Both paths reach the same effect -- g.status = 'APPROVED' -- which is the one-sentence check WEB-24 asks for.
The @Pattern on status narrows the value to four literals, one of which is exactly the privileged one.

findings.unaided_label: PUT sets APPROVED without approver role

findings.title: Kafka consumer writes grants with none of the validation or authorization the REST path applies
findings.evidence: GrantEntity has two writers. The REST writer (GrantResource.create/update) goes through @Valid GrantPayload with @Size, @DecimalMin("0.00"), @DecimalMax("5000000.00") and @Pattern("DRAFT|SUBMITTED|APPROVED|REJECTED") (GrantResource.java:36-42) and through AuthzFilter. The event writer calls repo.applyEvent with new BigDecimal(grant.getString("amount","0")), grant.getString("dept","programmes") and grant.getString("status","DRAFT") (lines 43-47) -- no bean validation, no status allowlist, no amount ceiling, no authorization filter (it is not a JAX-RS request). writer_parity.py flagged this service family as the composition shape it looks for.
findings.impact: Anyone able to publish to grants.events.v2 sets any grant's amount above the 5,000,000 ceiling or to a negative number, moves it to an arbitrary department, and sets status straight to APPROVED -- bypassing the grants.approver role entirely. A malformed amount also throws NumberFormatException outside the guarded block, poisoning the consumer.
findings.recommendation: Deserialize the event into the same GrantPayload record and run the same validator before applyEvent; authenticate and authorize the producer at the topic; wrap the BigDecimal parse and route failures to a dead-letter topic.

triage.reason: No shared validation layer covers both writers: the constraints live on the JAX-RS payload record, which the consumer never constructs.
The topic is not a bounded internal channel in any way this repository evidences: application.properties:23-27 configures the connector but no authentication, ACL or mTLS.
A second principal is crossed: the case management system is a distinct producer and the consumer trusts its payload wholesale.

findings.title: Attachment download does not check that the caller may see the named grant
findings.evidence: download(@PathParam("grantId") long grantId, @PathParam("name") String name) uses grantId only to build the storage directory at line 46. The injected GrantRepository field (line 39) is never used in this method, and no department, ownership or entitlement comparison is performed before Files.copy streams the file at line 52.
findings.impact: A caller who knows or enumerates a grant id (sequential longs) downloads that grant's signed award letter and due diligence pack. With the missing @Authorized annotation above, no credential is needed either.
findings.recommendation: Load the grant, compare its dept against the caller's entitlement (or ask the policy sidecar with the resource identity), and 404 on mismatch.

triage.reason: The name-bound AuthzFilter does not apply to this class at all, so there is no layer performing the check.
Signed award letters and due diligence packs are, per the class docstring at lines 27-30, exactly the sensitive documents of the domain.
grantId is a path parameter chosen freely by the caller; the long type constrains its form, not its ownership.

findings.title: Auditor policy rule guards a path no route serves
findings.evidence: path_coverage.py joined the mounted routes against the paths the guards claim to cover and reported: DEAD GUARD '/api/grants/audit' guards nothing: no route starts with it [policy/authz.rego:23]. Confirming by reading, the only JAX-RS paths under /api/grants are '' (list), '{id}', '{id}/approve', 'publications' and 'public/register'; nothing serves /api/grants/audit/.
findings.impact: The auditor entitlement is inert: programme auditors cannot in fact read the audit trail, and the rule creates a false impression that a cross-department read path is governed. If the route is added later under a slightly different name the rule stays silent, and if it is added under this name it grants every auditor read across all departments with no further review.
findings.recommendation: Either remove the rule, or add the route it was written for and cover it with a test that fails when the rule and the route drift apart.

triage.reason: The rule is in the shipped bundle policy, not a fixture; what is absent is the route, which is the finding.

Impact reaches users in both directions: programme auditors are denied the cross-department read the policy claims to grant them, and the rule is a latent over-grant that will silently allow every auditor a cross-department read the day a route is added under that prefix. Severity is low because neither effect is exploitable today.
There is no alternative reading: startswith(input.resource.path, "/api/grants/audit/") is compared against paths that never begin that way.

findings.title: Debug bypass rule left in the shipped authorization policy
findings.evidence: authz.rego contains `allow if { input.debug_bypass == true }` with a comment (lines 32-33) saying it is retained for the policy playground. The bundle containing it is the same one the sidecar loads in production, per application.properties:8-9.
findings.impact: Any caller of the decision API whose input document carries debug_bypass: true is allowed unconditionally. This service's own OpaClient.inputFor (OpaClient.java:79-94) builds the document field by field and never sets that key, so it is not reachable through grant-policy's own HTTP surface; it is reachable by anything else that queries the same sidecar or the same published bundle with a caller-influenced input document.
findings.recommendation: Delete the rule from the shipped bundle and keep it in a playground-only overlay, or gate it on a data document value that is only present in a non-production bundle.

triage.reason: The construct is not narrower than it reads within the policy itself: the rule has no guard at all. The narrowing that does exist is in a different component (OpaClient.inputFor never sets the key), which is FP-02 territory and is answered UNKNOWN there because other consumers of the same bundle are out of scope.
The rule is inside the authorization decision itself, so no layer sits behind it to compensate.
Whether any other consumer of this bundle forwards a caller-influenced input document is not establishable from this tree, which is why this is probable rather than confirmed.

findings.title: Legacy adjustment route reaches the admin controller on a path the admin guard does not match
findings.evidence: ApplicationController gates the admin area with before_action :require_admin, if: :admin_area? (line 8), and admin_area? is request.path.start_with?("/api/v1/admin") (line 29). routes.rb:30 maps POST /api/v1/invoices/:invoice_id/adjust to admin/adjustments#create -- the same controller action as the canonical /api/v1/admin/adjustments route at line 23 -- but its request path begins /api/v1/invoices, so admin_area? is false and require_admin never runs. The routing comment at lines 26-29 states plainly that nothing else had to change when the canonical route moved under /admin, which is the defect.
findings.impact: Any authenticated partner posts arbitrary monetary corrections against invoices without the admin role. Per the controller comment at lines 17-19, this is the one place a partner can move money that has already been posted.
findings.recommendation: Key the admin gate on the controller/module rather than the request path (for example a before_action in Api::V1::Admin::BaseController), so any route that reaches the action inherits it. Then delete or explicitly gate the legacy alias.

triage.reason: require_admin is the compensating control and its trigger condition is exactly what this route sidesteps; there is no second admin check inside AdjustmentsController.
The reverse of FP-11: the guard applies to less than it appears to, because it is keyed on a path prefix and not on the code it protects.
The route is declared unconditionally in config/routes.rb with no environment guard.

findings.title: Adjustment creation loads the invoice without the caller's organisation scope
findings.evidence: index scopes correctly with .where(invoices: { org_id: current_user.org_id }) at line 8. create calls Invoice.find(invoice_id) at line 21, with invoice_id taken from params[:invoice_id] or the permitted adjustment params (lines 38-40) and no org comparison anywhere before Adjustment.create! and LedgerPosting#credit! run at lines 24-31. ApplicationController#scoped_invoices exists at line 46 for exactly this and is not used here.
findings.impact: A partner posts an adjustment against any invoice in any organisation, moving money on another tenant's ledger. Combined with the route alias above, without the admin role either.
findings.recommendation: Load through scoped_invoices.find(invoice_id) so an out-of-org id raises RecordNotFound and is rendered as 404 by the handler at line 10.

triage.reason: No default scope or multi-tenant middleware is present: scoping in this codebase is done explicitly per query via scoped_invoices, which this action does not call.
The construct is not narrower than it reads: Invoice.find searches the whole table, and the sibling index in the same file shows the author knew the scope was needed.
A second principal is crossed: the invoice belongs to another org.

findings.title: Invoice update loads the invoice without the caller's organisation scope
findings.evidence: index (line 7), show (line 16), create (line 21) and void (line 44) all go through scoped_invoices, which filters by current_user.org_id (application_controller.rb:47). update alone calls Invoice.find(params[:id]) at line 34 and then invoice.update(invoice_params), where invoice_params permits reference, memo, amount_cents, currency, issued_on and posted_at (lines 52-54). writer_parity.py flagged this same method as the writer whose sibling checks and which does not.
findings.impact: Any authenticated partner rewrites any other organisation's invoice, including its amount_cents and currency. The comment at lines 31-32 ('this stays open for the whole life of the invoice') describes the field policy and hides that the row is not scoped.
findings.recommendation: Use scoped_invoices.find(params[:id]) here as every sibling action does, and add a request spec that has org A attempt to update org B's invoice and expect 404.

triage.reason: There is no mandatory tenant scope: scoping is explicit per query in this codebase and this query omits it.
There is no benign reading -- the four sibling actions in the same file use the scoped relation and this one uses the bare model.
The second principal is the owning organisation of the invoice being rewritten.

findings.title: Export ordering is built by string interpolation inside Arel.sql, giving SQL injection
findings.evidence: column comes from params[:sort].presence (line 16) with no allowlist. direction is constrained to ASC/DESC by the ternary at line 15, but column is not. The two are joined and wrapped in Arel.sql, which is precisely the call that tells Rails to skip its raw-SQL ordering protection, and handed to .order (line 19). The comment at lines 12-13 documents that sort is passed through on purpose.
findings.impact: An authenticated partner injects arbitrary SQL into the ORDER BY clause of a query over the invoices table -- subquery-based data extraction across organisations, and on PostgreSQL, expression evaluation. The org scope on the SELECT does not constrain what an injected ORDER BY subquery can read.
findings.recommendation: Map params[:sort] through an allowlist of permitted column names (the pattern already used correctly in parcel-track's sort_column) and pass only the resulting literal to Arel.sql, or use .order(hash_form) which Rails validates.

triage.reason: params[:sort] reaches the sink with only .presence applied; there is no allowlist, cast or constraint between the request and Arel.sql.
The sink is the query text itself, and Arel.sql exists specifically to mark a string as trusted so Rails will not sanitise it.
The narrowing that does exist covers the other operand: direction is allowlisted and column is not, in the same interpolation.

findings.title: Export listing and re-download serve any organisation's export file
findings.evidence: index returns Dir.children(EXPORT_ROOT).sort -- every file in tmp/exports, across all organisations -- with no filter. stream (lines 28-33) builds EXPORT_ROOT.join("#{params[:path]}.csv") and send_file's it after only a File.exist? check; there is no org, ownership or manifest lookup anywhere in the action. The filenames are partly caller-chosen through safe_filename (line 48), so index hands an attacker the exact names stream will accept.
findings.impact: Any authenticated partner enumerates every export ever written and downloads them, obtaining other organisations' full invoice ledgers (reference, memo, amount_cents, currency, status, issued_on).
findings.recommendation: Record exports in a table keyed by org, scope both index and stream through current_user.org_id, and store the files under a per-org directory with server-generated names.

triage.reason: No layer scopes these two actions: require_admin does not apply (the path is /api/v1/exports) and scoped_invoices is not involved in either action.
The files are CSV ledgers of invoices, which the rest of the controller treats as org-private.
The route constraint at routes.rb:18 narrows the filename charset; it narrows nothing about whose file it is.

findings.title: Bulk import takes the organisation id from the uploaded CSV row
findings.evidence: build_row sets org_id: row["org_id"].presence || upload.org_id. The CSV is partner-supplied (the class comment at lines 3-4 says the partner drops it on the upload endpoint), so a row that carries an org_id column overrides the uploading partner's own organisation, which is the only trustworthy value available at line 31.
findings.impact: A partner writes invoices into any other organisation's ledger by adding one column to the file it already uploads. Every read path in the API scopes by org_id, so the injected rows are then visible to and actionable by the victim organisation.
findings.recommendation: Ignore any org_id present in the file and always use upload.org_id; if a legitimate multi-org import exists, authorize each target org explicitly against the uploader.

triage.reason: row["org_id"] is read from the uploaded file body with no allowlist or comparison against upload.org_id.
insert_all (line 19) bypasses model callbacks and validations, so Invoice's own issuer_belongs_to_org validation (invoice.rb:31) never runs on this path.
The second principal is the organisation whose ledger receives the rows.

findings.title: Bulk import writes rows with insert_all, skipping every model validation and callback
findings.evidence: Invoice.insert_all(rows, returning: false) writes straight to the table. Invoice declares uniqueness of reference scoped to org_id, numericality greater_than: 0 on amount_cents, inclusion for currency and status, the issuer_belongs_to_org validation and the assert_ledger_balanced before_save (invoice.rb:8-15) -- none of which insert_all executes. build_row also coerces amount_cents with .to_i (line 34), turning any non-numeric value silently into 0.
findings.impact: Imported rows can carry a negative or zero amount, a currency outside USD/EUR/GBP/CAD, a status outside the four allowed values, or a duplicate reference within an org -- states the rest of the application and the month-end trial balance assume cannot exist.
findings.recommendation: Validate each row against the model (or a dedicated schema object) before batching, and keep the batched write only for rows that passed; alternatively add matching database-level constraints so the fast path cannot produce an invalid row.

triage.reason: The validations are the control and insert_all is documented to skip them; no database constraint is declared in the tree to compensate.
The invariants are load-bearing: assert_ledger_balanced exists (per its comment at lines 37-38) to stop the trial balance drifting.
Every field in build_row originates in the uploaded CSV.

findings.title: Credit posting writes the invoice amount with update_columns, skipping validations and the balance assertion
findings.evidence: credit! computes @invoice.amount_cents - amount_cents and writes it with update_columns (lines 32-35), which skips validations, callbacks and the before_save assert_ledger_balanced. The sibling void! on line 22 uses update!, which runs them. The amount reaching credit! is Integer(adjustment_params[:amount_cents]) from adjustments_controller.rb:22, and Integer() accepts negative values, so a negative adjustment increases the invoice amount.
findings.impact: An adjustment can drive amount_cents to zero or negative, or above the sum of its ledger entries, both of which the model's numericality validation and balance assertion exist to prevent. The comment at lines 26-28 also confirms the write deliberately avoids the audit feed's updated_at signal, so the change is not surfaced to subscribers.
findings.recommendation: Use update! so the model invariants run, reject non-positive amount_cents at the controller boundary, and if the audit feed must not fire, suppress it explicitly rather than by skipping the whole callback chain.

triage.reason: The model validations are the control and update_columns is defined to bypass them; there is no database CHECK constraint in the tree.
amount_cents comes from the request body via permitted params; Integer() constrains the type, not the sign or the magnitude.
The bypassed check is the primary integrity control for posted money, not a redundant one.

findings.title: Token issuance and refresh endpoints are not covered by any throttle
findings.class: missing rate limiting on an authentication endpoint
findings.evidence: Enumerating the initializer key by key: three throttles are declared, matching /api/v1/invoices (line 18), /api/v1/exports (line 22) and /api/v1/admin (line 25). routes.rb:5-6 places the credential exchange at /api/v1/tokens and /api/v1/tokens/refresh, which match none of the three prefixes. TokensController additionally skips authentication for both actions (tokens_controller.rb:4), and no lockout, backoff or attempt counter exists in the controller.
findings.impact: Partner client_secret values and refresh tokens can be brute-forced at full request rate against an unauthenticated endpoint, with no throttle and no per-identity lockout. The endpoints that are throttled are the ones behind authentication; the one that grants it is not.
findings.recommendation: Add a throttle keyed on client_id (not only on IP) for /api/v1/tokens and /api/v1/tokens/refresh, plus an exponential backoff or lockout per client_id after repeated failures.

triage.reason: Rack::Attack is the only rate-limiting layer in the repository and its three throttle blocks provably do not match this path.
An upstream WAF or API gateway could throttle it, but no such configuration was provided; per FP-08 that is UNKNOWN, so the finding stands rather than being ruled out.
The safelist at line 13 is correctly narrowed by Rails.env.test?, so it is not the cause; the gap is a missing throttle, not an over-wide exemption.

findings.title: Exported CSV cells are written without neutralising spreadsheet formula prefixes
findings.evidence: to_csv writes HEADERS.map { |h| invoice.public_send(h) } straight into CSV.generate. Two of the six exported attributes -- reference and memo -- are partner-controlled through invoice_params (invoices_controller.rb:52-54) and through the bulk import (bulk_import_job.rb:32-33), and neither is prefixed, quoted or escaped against leading =, +, - or @.
findings.impact: A partner stores a memo beginning with = and the finance team's spreadsheet evaluates it on open. In Excel this reaches DDE/external-data prompts and, with a single click-through, command execution on the finance workstation that downloaded the file.
findings.recommendation: Prefix any cell whose first character is one of = + - @ tab or CR with a single quote (or wrap it), applied centrally in to_csv so every exported column is covered.

triage.reason: reference and memo originate from partner-supplied request bodies and uploaded CSVs.
The sink is dangerous in the form it is reached: send_data with type text/csv and a .csv filename is the form spreadsheet software evaluates.
No compensating control exists downstream in the repository; the mitigation would have to live in the consuming spreadsheet, which is not evidenced.

findings.title: Label download joins a caller-controlled tail path onto the storage root
findings.evidence: The route pattern is #[get("/labels/{shipment_id}/{label_ref:.*}")] (line 22) -- a tail match that captures path separators. label_ref is joined onto state.cfg.label_root at line 39 and read with fs::read at line 40 with no canonicalisation and no containment check against label_root. download_name (lines 13-20) does squeeze the value to word characters, but it is applied only to the Content-Disposition header at line 46, never to the path at line 39: the sanitiser exists and is applied to the wrong value.
findings.impact: Any authenticated account holding one of its own shipments reads arbitrary files the service user can open -- /etc/passwd, the process environment via /proc/self/environ (which carries CARRIER_KEY and DATABASE_URL), and mounted secrets. Rust's Path::join also replaces the base entirely if label_ref is absolute.
findings.recommendation: Resolve the joined path with canonicalize() and reject anything that does not start with label_root, or better, look the label reference up in the database and derive a server-side filename from the row.

triage.reason: The only control on this path is the shipment ownership check at lines 30-37, which gates whether the handler runs at all -- it does not constrain label_ref.
The sanitiser looks like the narrowing condition but applies to a different value: download_name(&label_ref) feeds the header, while &label_ref itself feeds the join.
label_ref is the request path tail, unconstrained by the route pattern .* .

findings.title: Bulk import writes attachment files at a caller-chosen path
findings.evidence: stage_attachment does root.join(name) with name coming straight from BulkRow::attachment_name in the request body (line 64), then create_dir_all on the parent (line 78) and fs::write of attachment_body (line 81). There is no basename extraction, no canonicalisation and no containment check against import_root. In Rust, Path::join with an absolute component discards the base entirely, so "/etc/cron.d/x" writes to /etc/cron.d/x, and "../../.." traverses.
findings.impact: Any authenticated account writes arbitrary content to arbitrary filesystem paths as the service user, creating intermediate directories as needed. That reaches code execution through any path the runtime or the host reads back (cron fragments, an ssh authorized_keys, a config file, a systemd unit) and, at minimum, overwrites the label store that handlers/labels.rs serves.
findings.recommendation: Derive the stored filename server-side (a uuid), or take only Path::file_name(name), then canonicalize the result and assert it is inside import_root before writing. Bound attachment_body size explicitly.

triage.reason: No containment check exists anywhere on the path; the only validation in bulk_import is the row-count check at line 39.
attachment_name is a plain Option<String> deserialized from the request body with no serde validation.
The boundary crossed is the service's own filesystem trust boundary, and the writer is any API-key holder.

findings.title: Webhook subscription update does not check that the subscription belongs to the caller
findings.evidence: create_subscription compares body.account_id against principal.account_id and returns 403 on mismatch (lines 26-28). update_subscription performs no such check: it takes the numeric id from the path (line 50), validates only the URL, and calls store.update_subscription (line 56), whose statement is `update webhook_subscriptions set callback_url = $2, events = $3 where id = $1` (store.rs:164-167) with no account_id predicate. The principal is used only in the log line at line 60.
findings.impact: Any authenticated account enumerates sequential subscription ids and repoints another account's webhook at a server it controls, receiving that account's live scan events (shipment references and state transitions) and silencing the victim's own integration.
findings.recommendation: Add `and account_id = $4` to the update statement and bind principal.account_id, returning 404 when rows_affected is zero; mirror the create handler's explicit ownership comparison.

triage.reason: AuthGuard establishes who the caller is but performs no object-level scoping; there is no ORM-level tenant filter in this codebase.
The sibling handler in the same file performs exactly the check this one omits, on the same table.
The SubscriptionPayload struct carries account_id, but update_subscription never reads it -- the field that would narrow the write is present and unused.

findings.title: SSRF allowlist checks only literal addresses and misses several private ranges
findings.evidence: validate_callback_url blocks the literal hostnames localhost, *.internal and *.cluster.local (line 45) and, when host_str parses as an IP literal, v4.is_private() || is_loopback() || is_link_local() or v6.is_loopback() || is_unspecified() (lines 49-57). It never resolves the hostname, so any name that resolves to a private address passes. Among literals it also misses IPv4 0.0.0.0 (is_unspecified, which routes to localhost on Linux), the shared/CGNAT range 100.64.0.0/10, IPv6 unique-local fc00::/7, and IPv4-mapped IPv6 such as ::ffff:169.254.169.254.
findings.impact: The docstring at lines 32-33 states callbacks are fired from inside the delivery VPC and a subscriber must not be able to point one at something only reachable from in there. A subscriber registers an attacker-controlled hostname whose A record is 169.254.169.254 or an internal address and the service issues requests from its VPC position -- cloud metadata credentials and internal APIs.
findings.recommendation: Resolve the host, apply the range checks to every resolved address, re-apply them after every redirect (or disable redirects), and prefer an explicit allowlist of subscriber domains. Pin the resolved address for the actual connection to close the DNS-rebinding window.

triage.reason: No egress proxy or network policy is evidenced in the repository; this function is the only egress control present.
The narrowing that exists is real but incomplete, and the gap is in the same block: the IP branch runs only when host_str parses as an IP, which a hostname never does.
callback_url is supplied by the subscriber on both create paths.

findings.title: Carrier webhook signature is compared with a non-constant-time equality
findings.class: timing side channel on signature verification
findings.evidence: The expected HMAC-SHA256 is hex-encoded at line 90 and compared with `if provided != expected`, a plain &str inequality that short-circuits at the first differing byte. Every other comparison of a secret in this tree is either constant-time (session-broker/session/cookie.ts:23) or a database lookup on a digest.
findings.impact: An attacker who can submit callbacks for a known account_id learns the expected signature byte by byte from response-time differences, then forges scan events that flip shipment states in that account's ledger. The account_id is a path parameter, so the endpoint is reachable without any credential.
findings.recommendation: Compare with a constant-time primitive -- prefer mac.verify_slice(&hex::decode(provided)?) from the hmac crate, which is constant-time and also rejects malformed hex.

triage.reason: The comparison is the security decision itself, not an incidental string equality.
There is no other verification of the callback: this comparison is the whole control, so it is load-bearing rather than defence in depth.

No out-of-repository control is claimed or plausible for this defect: the comparison operator is the whole of it, and no proxy, gateway or platform setting turns a short-circuiting string equality into a constant-time one.

findings.title: Unauthenticated tracking status endpoint returns the recipient's full contact details
findings.class: excessive data exposure on an unauthenticated endpoint
findings.evidence: auth.rs:23-24 treats any path ending in /status as open, so no API key is required. The handler calls store.get_shipment_any_account(id) (line 135), which deliberately drops the account predicate (store.rs:105-113) and selects SHIPMENT_COLUMNS -- the same projection used by the authenticated endpoints, including recipient_name, recipient_address and recipient_phone (store.rs:23-24). The whole ShipmentView is serialized to the response at line 136.
findings.impact: Anyone holding or guessing a shipment id retrieves the recipient's name, full postal address and phone number with no credential. The comment at lines 20-22 justifies the open endpoint for the recipient's own tracking page, but the response carries far more than a tracking page needs.
findings.recommendation: Return a narrowed projection for this endpoint -- id, state and last_scan_at only -- and keep the contact block behind the authenticated handlers. Consider a per-shipment tracking token rather than the raw id.

triage.reason: The exposure is intended only as far as showing a delivery state; the finding moves to what sits behind that intended exposure, which is the contact block, exactly as FP-05 directs.
Recipient name, address and phone are personal data by any reading of PRV-01.
Nothing narrows the projection: get_shipment_any_account reuses the same SHIPMENT_COLUMNS constant as the authenticated queries.

findings.title: API key scopes are loaded and never enforced anywhere
findings.evidence: Principal carries scopes: Vec<String> (line 15) and store.rs:35-44 selects the scopes column and populates it. Grepping the whole crate for `scopes` returns exactly three hits -- the struct field, the SELECT and the row.get -- and no comparison, no membership test and no gate. Every handler authorizes on account_id alone or not at all.
findings.impact: The per-key scope model exists in the schema and in the type system and constrains nothing: a read-only integration key can create shipments, run bulk imports and rewrite webhook subscriptions. Operators granting narrow scopes get no narrowing.
findings.recommendation: Add a scope requirement to each route (a guard extractor or a middleware taking the required scope) and fail closed when the key's scopes do not contain it; add a test per route asserting the wrong scope is rejected.

triage.reason: There is no other authorization layer to carry the same decision: AuthGuard resolves identity only, and the handlers check account_id at most.
An upstream API gateway could enforce scopes, but no such configuration was provided; the in-repo enforcement is provably absent.
It is not a redundant defence: nothing else implements per-key least privilege.

findings.title: Bulk import bounds the row count but not the attachment payload
findings.evidence: The only limit is body.shipments.len() > state.cfg.bulk_limit (default 2000, config.rs:44-47). Each BulkRow also carries attachment_body: String with #[serde(default)] and no length bound (lines 26-27), and every one of them is written to disk in the loop at lines 63-69 with no aggregate size accounting. No actix PayloadConfig or JsonConfig limit is registered in main.rs.
findings.impact: A single authenticated request stages up to bulk_limit attachment bodies of whatever size actix's default JSON limit permits, and repeated requests fill the import volume. Combined with the caller-chosen path above, the same loop is the write primitive.
findings.recommendation: Register an explicit web::JsonConfig limit in main.rs, cap attachment_body per row and in aggregate, and account for total staged bytes per account.

triage.reason: No payload limit is configured on the App in main.rs; the framework default is the only bound and it is not declared here.

The framework default bounds one request, not the aggregate: the loop writes every attachment to disk, so repeated requests still fill the import volume, which no per-request limit addresses. Severity is low because the per-request ceiling makes it slow rather than instant.
An ingress body-size limit would bound it further but none was provided.

findings.title: The entire admin router is mounted with no session or scope middleware
findings.evidence: profileRouter.use(requireSession) is applied at line 46 before profileRouter is mounted at line 47. adminRouter is mounted at line 50 with no equivalent line anywhere -- neither in main.ts nor inside routes/admin.ts, which imports nothing from the middleware module. Its three routes (admin.ts:12, 21, 26) read ctx.request/ctx.params directly and never touch ctx.state.session. requireScope, defined for exactly this purpose at middleware/require_session.ts:37, has zero call sites in the tree.
findings.impact: Anyone who can reach the service lists every live session for any org (with userId, orgId, roles and scopes), revokes any session by id, and signs out an entire organisation. That is unauthenticated account takeover reconnaissance plus denial of service against every user in an org.
