findings.recommendation: Apply requireSession and requireScope("sessions:read") / requireScope("sessions:revoke") to adminRouter before mounting it, and add a test that an unauthenticated request to each admin route returns 401.

triage.reason: No mandatory layer covers it: the two app-level middlewares registered before the routers are a CORS handler (line 11) and a Host allowlist (line 18), neither of which authenticates.
The exposure is not bounded: adminRouter is mounted on the same Application and the same listener as the public auth routes.
The mount is unconditional in buildApp, which is what import.meta.main runs at line 56.

findings.title: Unsigned legacy cookies are accepted, defeating cookie signature verification entirely
findings.evidence: The session id is resolved as (await verify(raw)) ?? decodeLegacy(raw). decodeLegacy (session/cookie.ts:53-56) splits on '|' and returns parts[1] whenever there are exactly two parts and the second is non-empty -- it performs no verification of any kind, as its own docstring at lines 49-52 states ('a plain "<user>|<session>" pair with no signature'). Any cookie value that fails HMAC verification therefore gets a second, unauthenticated chance.
findings.impact: An attacker who learns or guesses a session id sends nw_sid=x|<sessionid> and is authenticated as that user without possessing any signing key. The signature scheme in cookie.ts is fully bypassable for the price of one pipe character.
findings.recommendation: Remove the legacy fallback. If a migration window is genuinely required, gate it on an explicit expiry date and on the cookie carrying a distinguishing legacy marker, and require re-authentication rather than trusting the value.

triage.reason: loadSession (line 27) confirms the id exists in Redis but proves nothing about who presented it; existence is not authentication.
The fallback is unconditional in the shipped middleware -- no flag, no environment check, no expiry.
This is not a redundant control: the HMAC is the only thing binding a cookie to the server, and this line makes it optional.

findings.title: Session identifiers are generated from Math.random
findings.evidence: newSessionId builds a 32-character hex string from Math.floor(Math.random() * 16) in a loop. Math.random is a non-cryptographic PRNG (xorshift128+ in V8, which Deno uses), whose internal state is recoverable from a modest number of observed outputs, after which past and future outputs are computable. The docstring at lines 51-55 justifies it on the grounds that ids only need to be unique within the TTL and are re-signed before leaving the process.
findings.impact: An attacker who obtains a few session ids -- for example by opening several sessions of their own, or by reading the unauthenticated /admin/sessions listing above -- recovers the generator state and predicts other users' session ids. Combined with the unsigned legacy cookie path, a predicted id is directly usable as a valid session with no signing key.
findings.recommendation: Generate ids with crypto.getRandomValues (or crypto.randomUUID) with at least 128 bits of entropy. The re-signing argument in the docstring does not hold, because the legacy path accepts an unsigned cookie.

triage.reason: The value is a security token: it is the sole key to a session record in Redis, so its unpredictability is load-bearing.
The claimed compensating control is the HMAC re-signing, which cookie.ts's legacy path (line 53) makes optional -- so it does not cover the path to the sink.
There is no benign reading: the output of newSessionId is used directly as the session key at line 72 and 82.

findings.title: The remember-me cookie is written without HttpOnly, Secure or SameSite
findings.evidence: setSessionCookie (session/cookie.ts:62-75) is described in its docstring as 'the single place that knows how a session cookie is shaped' and sets httpOnly, secure and sameSite: 'lax'. The remember-me branch at auth.ts:35-39 bypasses it and calls ctx.cookies.set directly with only path, domain and maxAge -- none of the three protective attributes. The comment at lines 32-34 says this was done because the helper pins the lifetime to the session TTL.
findings.impact: The thirty-day session cookie is readable by any script on the domain (so any XSS becomes persistent account takeover), is transmitted over plaintext HTTP, and is attached to cross-site requests, making every state-changing endpoint CSRF-able for users who ticked 'keep me signed in'.
findings.recommendation: Give setSessionCookie the ttlSeconds argument it already accepts (it is parameterised at cookie.ts:65) and call it with config.rememberTtlSeconds, deleting the ad-hoc set entirely.

triage.reason: No layer re-writes Set-Cookie: the only app-level middlewares are CORS and the Host allowlist, neither of which touches cookie attributes.
The sibling helper in the same codebase sets all three attributes for the same cookie name, which settles the reading.
The branch runs whenever the login body carries remember: true, in the shipped handler.

findings.title: Profile cache key is not scoped to the viewer, so a privileged view is served to unprivileged callers
findings.evidence: viewFor (lines 24-50) returns either a base view or one enriched with email, phone, mfaEnrolled and recoveryCodesLeft depending on the requesting session -- self, support with an open ticket in the same org, or the sessions:read scope. The result is cached under profileKey(id) = `profile:v2:${id}` (store.ts:129-131), which contains only the subject's id and nothing about the viewer, and is read back at line 57 before any authorization runs. The PATCH handler writes the same viewer-dependent view under the same key at line 100.
findings.impact: As soon as one privileged viewer (or the subject themselves) loads a profile, the enriched view -- including the number of remaining recovery codes and the enrolled phone -- is served for fifteen minutes to any signed-in caller who requests that profile, regardless of role, scope or organisation.
findings.recommendation: Cache the record, not the view: memoise loadProfile under profileKey(id) and run viewFor on every request; or include the viewer's identity and entitlement in the cache key.

triage.reason: No narrowing condition survives on the cache path: line 58 returns the cached body before viewFor is ever consulted.
viewFor is the compensating control and the cache read at line 57 short-circuits it.
The enriched fields are personal data and account-recovery state, not public content.

findings.title: Every member holds profile:write, so the profile ownership check never rejects
findings.evidence: The guard is `if (session.userId !== id && !hasScope(session.scopes, "profile:write"))`. SCOPES_BY_ROLE (store.ts:44-49) grants profile:write to the member role -- the baseline role -- as well as to admin. mintSession (line 69) unions the scopes of the user's roles onto the session. Since every ordinary user is a member, the second operand is false for essentially every session, so the conjunction never fires. There is no organisation comparison in the guard either.
findings.impact: Any signed-in user PATCHes any other user's profile in any organisation, rewriting displayName and phone. The rewritten record is then written to `directory:${id}` with a 365-day TTL (line 99), so it also poisons the directory source of truth that loadProfile reads, and simultaneously overwrites the cached view.
findings.recommendation: Remove profile:write from the member role (self-service edits are already permitted by the userId equality), scope the check to the caller's org, and treat profile:write as an operator capability. Add a test in which a member PATCHes another member and expects 403.

triage.reason: requireSession establishes identity only and no other layer restricts which profile id may be written; the guard on this line is the only one on the path.
The handler and the role table are both shipped source with no flag or environment guard.
The check looks like a narrowing condition but narrows nothing, because the scope it tests for is held by the default role.

findings.title: Sign-in continuation redirects to any caller-supplied target
findings.evidence: authRouter.get("/continue") reads the `next` query parameter and passes it straight to ctx.response.redirect (lines 60-61). There is no scheme check, no host allowlist and no requirement that the value be a relative path; the default "/dashboard" shows the intended shape.
findings.impact: The identity provider's post-sign-in landing URL sends the freshly authenticated user to an attacker-chosen origin. That is a credible phishing primitive on the accounts hostname, and it forwards any token or referrer the flow carries in the query string.
findings.recommendation: Accept only same-origin relative paths: reject any value that does not start with a single '/' (and is not '//'), or resolve it against the canonical origin and compare hosts against config.allowedHosts.

triage.reason: next is read directly from ctx.request.url.searchParams with no validation.
The Host allowlist middleware at main.ts:18 constrains the inbound Host header, not the outbound Location value.
There is no server-side equivalent check elsewhere; this handler is the whole redirect path.

findings.title: Password reset link is built from the part of the Host header the allowlist does not inspect
findings.evidence: The allowlist middleware compares (host ?? "").split(":")[0] against config.allowedHosts (main.ts:19-21) -- everything after the first colon is discarded before the comparison. The reset handler then reads the raw header again at auth.ts:74 and interpolates the whole value into the link at line 75. A value such as `accounts.northwind.test:1@evil.invalid` passes the allowlist as `accounts.northwind.test` and produces `https://accounts.northwind.test:1@evil.invalid/auth/reset/confirm?token=...`, in which everything before the @ is URL userinfo and the real host is the attacker's.
findings.impact: A password reset requested for a victim's address emails them a link that resolves to the attacker's host while displaying the legitimate hostname, handing over the reset token when clicked. queueResetEmail logs only new URL(link).pathname (line 81), so the token itself is not leaked to the log -- the exposure is entirely through the email.
findings.recommendation: Never build outbound links from the Host header: use a configured canonical origin (config.allowedHosts[0]) unconditionally. If the header must be used, validate the full value, not a prefix of it.

triage.reason: Whether Deno/oak or a fronting proxy rejects a Host header containing '@' before the handler sees it is not establishable from this tree, and no proxy configuration was provided. UNKNOWN caps this at probable.
The narrowing condition is real but applies to a different value than the one used: the allowlist inspects a prefix of the header and the link consumes the whole header.
A password reset token is a credential, not inert data.

findings.title: With no signing keys configured, cookie verification can never succeed and every request takes the unsigned path
findings.evidence: signingKeys() reads SESSION_SIGNING_KEYS with a `?? ""` fallback and then filters empties, so with the variable unset it returns []. verify (session/cookie.ts:43-46) iterates that array; with zero elements the loop body never runs and it returns null for every cookie. require_session.ts:21 then falls through to decodeLegacy for every request. sign (cookie.ts:31) destructures the same empty array, so the value passed as key material is undefined.
findings.impact: A deployment that forgets the variable does not fail loudly: it silently degrades to accepting unsigned `<anything>|<sessionid>` cookies for every request, which is the authentication bypass above with no attacker effort at all. The service never signals that its signing keys are missing.
findings.recommendation: Fail fast at start-up when signingKeys() is empty, and assert a non-empty key list in verify before deciding a cookie is invalid, so a configuration error becomes an outage rather than an open door.

triage.reason: The default is in the production config module and applies whenever the environment variable is absent.

Whether the deployment sets SESSION_SIGNING_KEYS is an out-of-repo fact with no artifact provided; the in-repo defect -- silent degradation rather than a hard failure -- is fully established regardless.
There is no start-up assertion, health check or other layer in the tree that would catch the empty key list.

findings.title: requireScope is defined and registered on nothing
findings.evidence: requireScope(scope) is exported at line 37 and builds a Middleware that 403s when hasScope fails. Grepping the whole tree for `requireScope` returns exactly one hit -- this definition. No router calls .use(requireScope(...)) and no route wraps a handler in it. The scope vocabulary it would enforce (sessions:read, sessions:revoke, keys:write) is fully defined in store.ts:44-49 and consumed nowhere except the one inline hasScope calls in profile.ts.
findings.impact: The per-scope authorization model exists in the type system and in the role table but governs nothing, which is why the admin router is reachable without sessions:read or sessions:revoke. An operator reading this file would reasonably conclude scope enforcement is present.
findings.recommendation: Register requireScope on the admin routes with the scope each one needs, and add a test per route asserting a session without the scope is rejected.

triage.reason: No other layer performs the scope decision; the only hasScope calls in the tree are the two inline ones in profile.ts, which cover neither admin route.
An upstream gateway could enforce scopes, but no configuration was provided; the in-repo absence is proven by grep.
The middleware is exported from a shipped module; what is missing is the registration, which is the finding.

findings.title: Login has no attempt limiting or lockout
findings.evidence: The login handler looks the user up, calls verifyPassword and returns 401 on failure (lines 19-27). There is no attempt counter, no per-identity backoff, no lockout and no CAPTCHA anywhere in the handler or in the middleware stack: the only app-level middlewares registered in main.ts are CORS (line 11), the Host allowlist (line 18) and the request logger (line 30). PBKDF2 with 210,000 iterations (store.ts:170) raises the per-attempt cost but does not bound the number of attempts.
findings.impact: Credentials can be stuffed or sprayed against the directory at whatever rate the service will answer. The reset endpoint at line 64 is likewise unlimited, so it can be used to mail-bomb a known address.
findings.recommendation: Add per-identity and per-source attempt counters with exponential backoff and a lockout, and rate-limit the reset endpoint on the submitted address.

triage.reason: No rate-limiting middleware exists in the tree; the middleware stack is enumerable in full at main.ts:11-40.
An edge WAF could throttle it, but no configuration was provided; per FP-08 that is UNKNOWN, so the finding stands.
The PBKDF2 cost factor slows each attempt but is not an attempt limit, so it does not reduce this to informational.

findings.title: Session cookie is scoped to the parent domain, sharing it with every subdomain
findings.evidence: cookieDomain defaults to ".northwind.test" -- a leading-dot parent-domain scope -- and is used for both the helper-set cookie (session/cookie.ts:71) and the remember-me cookie (routes/auth.ts:37), as well as for deletion (cookie.ts:78). The allowedHosts default is the single host accounts.northwind.test, so the cookie is deliberately broader than the service that issues it.
findings.impact: Every host under northwind.test receives the session cookie on every request and, if it can set cookies, can overwrite it (session fixation). One compromised or user-content subdomain therefore reaches every user's session, which host-only scoping would prevent.
findings.recommendation: Set the cookie host-only (omit domain) if the sibling services can obtain sessions another way, or enumerate the exact subdomains that need it and document why each does. Add the __Host- prefix where host-only scoping is viable.

triage.reason: The sharing is intentional but not bounded: no list of the subdomains meant to receive it exists in the repository, and allowedHosts names only one host.

The exposure itself is unconditional and immediate: the session cookie is transmitted to every host under northwind.test on every request. What requires a second condition is the escalation to takeover, which is why the severity is low rather than why the finding is informational.
Which subdomains exist under northwind.test is not establishable from this tree.
